CONTEXT: guardrails/ holds ~56 "check-*" gate scripts that run in pre-commit/pre-push/CI to catch defects. The owner wants a "census": for each gate, when did it last catch something REAL (not a self-test/fixture, an actual live defect in the repo's own history)?

FOR EACH of these 28 checks, determine its verdict using this evidence hierarchy (cheapest first, escalate only if needed):
1. `cd /Users/sashaabramovich/live-spec && git log --all --oneline -i --grep="<short-name-derived-from-check>"` — e.g. for check-suite-budget.sh try grep terms like "suite-budget", "suite budget". Look for commit messages describing a real fix that this gate caught.
2. Search /Users/sashaabramovich/live-spec/.live-spec/PROBLEMS.md and /Users/sashaabramovich/live-spec/.live-spec/*.md audit files (day1-census-checks.md, day1-census-rules.md, crisis-audit-2026-08-08.md, culling-plan-*.md, batch*-verdicts-*.md) — grep them for the check's name; several of these files look like exactly this kind of prior census — read any relevant matches, they may already have partial answers you can cite/confirm. Note: ROADMAP.md row 622 (in the repo, you may grep it directly: `grep -n 'check-suite-budget' /Users/sashaabramovich/live-spec/ROADMAP.md`) documents a live catch of check-suite-budget.sh in detail — use it if relevant to your slice.
3. Search docs/prover/ (`ls /Users/sashaabramovich/live-spec/docs/prover`, then grep -rl "<check-name>" in it) for prover records mentioning this gate catching something.
4. If nothing found via 1-3, do ONE targeted `git log --all --oneline -- guardrails/<checkfile>` to see if the gate itself was recently authored/modified (a check added very recently may legitimately have "never caught anything yet" as an honest answer, not a failure to search).

VERDICT per check (one of):
- живой (дата) — cite the most recent real catch with evidence (commit sha or file:line)
- молчит с <дата> — it caught something historically but not recently; cite the last catch and the fact no more recent one was found
- никогда не ловил — you searched and found no evidence of a real catch (only self-test/fixture triggers, if any)
- недостаточно данных — you searched but evidence is genuinely ambiguous/unavailable (be honest, don't force a verdict)

OUTPUT: plain Russian, compact table: check name | verdict | evidence (one line, cite source). Do not pad — if a check's evidence search comes up empty after a reasonable effort, say "никогда не ловил (поиск: <what you tried>)" rather than inventing something.

Budget ~80-100k tokens across all 28 checks (a few minutes of grep per check, not deep reads). Report your findings as your final message — do not write any files.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

The mechanical net is a ratcheted counter `guardrails/node_growth_counter.py` with its ratchet `guardrails/node-file-cap.json`, seeded at the tree's current count so the tree lands green and standing debt is admitted while any increase reds; the cap ratchets down only, a split lowering a file's count and its cap with it, the prose-debt cap's lesson carried whole [INV-164]. This ratchet rides the suite `tests/test_node_growth.py`, the sibling of the prose-debt cap, and takes no push-gate letter. The prover's architecture lens grows a seventh check, the growth re-ask: a file whose node count sits at its ratchet is read for whether its nodes still each earn their place. The design review carries the split proposal in its two-objects shape [INV-142], naming the over-grown file and the split it offers. A split is a structure change, carved by the architecture step alone and re-proven there [INV-37, INV-113]. The proposed number is two nodes per code file, set on the host's word at the first budget landing [INV-41], and INV-135's declared layers say what counts as a code file. Honest boundary: the counter reads the map as written, so an under-declared coarse map evades it, which the every-fact-owned-once backstop and the prover's re-prove walk answer. [INV-233]

- **Everything that can grow declares the number that bounds it, and a watcher reads it.** The owner pressed the point on 2026-07-17: when a thing just grows without end — a script, a spec, a test matrix — the system cannot do nothing. Row 390 asks whether a file holds one thing or several, where raw size is the wrong signal; this asks whether a thing has grown past what it may weigh, where size is the signal and needs its own declared number. INV-41 already states the shape — a measurable budget with its watcher — scoped to the architecture's quality budgets, and this lifts it to every growable artifact. The four large working documents, PRODUCT_SPEC.md, ROADMAP.md, TEST_MATRIX.md, and JOURNAL.md, each declare a byte ceiling with a recorded reason in `guardrails/doc-bounds.json`, and the watcher `guardrails/check-doc-bound.py` (gate z in the push chain) reds a doc past its ceiling. It composes with the rotation law [INV-209]: crossing the bound is what earns a rotation, and rotation is the remedy the red points to, so a doc rotated today — carrying a manifest that names an archive dated today — passes even over its ceiling, since the grooming that shrinks the live file back under the bound has just been applied, while a rotation from another day does not clear today's overflow. A ceiling rises only with a recorded reason: every declared entry carries a non-empty one, and a bound with none reds. The ceilings are seeded above the current file sizes with rotation headroom, measured 2026-07-18, so the gate never reds the already-large tree; the ratchet's direction is down, reset by rotation, and a silent creep up has no door. A growable artifact with no declared bound is the defect, whatever its kind, and the pack proposes the number per artifact kind while the host's word sets it [INV-41]. [INV-234]

- **The CI mirror carries every local gate the push gate runs.** The push gate lives twice: `guardrails/pre-push` runs it on the author's machine, and `.github/workflows/gates.yml` re-runs it in CI as the second net that covers any machine [M-5]. The CI file is maintained by hand, so it drifts the moment a gate is added locally and the mirror is not touched. This movement had to hand-sync gates p, q, and s, and the row 420 gate audit found gates h, k, and n still missing from CI, so a push a green CI would wave through could still fail the local gate (the owner asked for that audit in person, 2026-07-17 ~18:27). The gate `guardrails/check-ci-mirror.sh` (gate u in the push chain) reads the gate letters `pre-push` invokes — its `-- gate X:` markers — and the gate letters `gates.yml` invokes — the `gate X` tokens in its step names — and reds on any local gate letter absent from CI, naming the gate and the one fix. The set a CI checkout legitimately skips lives in one machine-readable place both the gate and a human read, `guardrails/ci-mirror.json`, each carve-out carrying the reason it stays out of CI: gate c is folded into the test suite, where `test_traceability.py` runs under the pytest step (gate b); gate k reads a gitignored local freeze baseline a fresh checkout does not carry; gate m compares installed personal hooks a CI checkout does not install; and gate v reads the personal-layer settings.json. A carve-out naming a letter that is no local gate is itself drift and reds. To reach compliance this row added the runnable gates h and n to `gates.yml`, and gate u represents itself there so it never reds on its own absence. This is a structural scan kin of config-health [INV-175]: config-health proves the installed hook matches its source, and this proves the CI mirror matches the source too. [INV-210]

- **The chat judges stay wired: the installed settings.json lists every judge the pack runs.** The prose judges live at the chat surface — `scissors-scan.py`, `answer-first-scan.py`, and `register-judge-collect.sh` on the Stop event, `clock-hook.sh`, `chat-law-hook.sh`, and `register-judge-report.sh` on the UserPromptSubmit event — and each runs only because `~/.claude/settings.json` lists it. config-health (gate m) proves the installed hook file matches its source, and its own text hands this residual to the row 420 audit by name: it does not yet prove settings.json still lists the judge entries, because settings.json is personal-layer. A judge whose file is present and correct still goes dark when its settings.json entry is gone, because the run comes from the entry and the file only supplies what the entry names. That is the no-verdict failure this movement hit, a register judge that delivered no verdict because it was never wired live; the owner named it the movement's worst near-miss when he asked for the audit (2026-07-17 ~18:27). The gate `guardrails/check-judge-listed.py` (gate v in the push chain) reads the wired-hook declaration `guardrails/judge-hooks.json`, which maps each hook to its settings.json surface, asserts every file under `hooks/` is classified there so a hook added later cannot escape the check, and asserts each wired hook is referenced in its surface's array in the installed settings.json; a wired hook missing from its array reds, naming the hook, the surface, and the fix. settings.json is personal-layer, so where it cannot be read — a CI checkout, a host without it — the gate stands down by name and never falsely passes, the way config-health skips a CI checkout, and gate v rides the CI carve-out list [INV-210] for that reason. This is a structural scan kin of config-health [INV-175]: that arm proves the hook file exists, and this arm proves the entry that runs it exists. [INV-211]

- **Every gate carries a known-red proof: a gate that cannot fail is a check that looks at nothing.** A gate reports green two ways — because the input was clean, or because the check never fires at all. The second is the hollow gate this movement had to rebuild: the authority-anchor gate shipped reporting green without reaching the surfaces it claimed to inspect (commit 8a0209f rebuilt it to read the surfaces and strike the live fabrication), and a worker's false "zero violations" was the same disease, a claim that protected nothing because nothing could make it fail. The owner asked for the gate audit that surfaced this class in person (2026-07-17 ~18:27). So every gate the push chain runs carries a known-red proof: a committed red-first test that drives that gate's own check to a non-zero exit, so the gate is shown to fire. The gate `guardrails/check-every-gate-can-fail.py` (gate w in the push chain) enumerates the gate letters `pre-push` invokes — the same `-- gate X:` markers gate u reads — and requires each to be classified in `guardrails/gate-red-proofs.json`: a `proof` names the red-first test `<file>::<function>` that reds the gate's check, tied to the gate by a `reds` token the proof file must reference; a `covered` entry names a gate that runs no independent check of its own and rides another gate's red, carrying the reason it holds no separate fixture — gate c, whose anchor-ownership assertion rides the pytest suite (gate b), is the one such entry, mirroring the carve-out `ci-mirror.json` already declares for c. A registered proof is verified by reading its structure, since the suite already runs it under gate b: the proof file exists, the named function is defined in it, the `reds` token appears there, and the function body carries a non-zero-exit assertion, so a bare "the gate ships" presence test cannot pass as a red proof. A gate marker classified nowhere reds the meta-gate, a covered entry with no reason reds, and a `cannot_red` map names any gate that by construction can never be made to fail so it reds loudly and stays surfaced. Run against the real chain at this landing, every gate that invokes a check already carried its red proof from its own landing, so nothing was back-filled. This is the guard over the guards, a structural scan kin of config-health [INV-175] and the CI-mirror gate [INV-210]. [INV-212]

- **A finished worker leaves no runaway child that burns unseen.** When a worker or task the run spawned completes, a descendant it left behind can keep burning a full core unnoticed. The instance the owner's memory holds (2026-07-17): a difflib process burned one core for forty-six minutes after its worker reported done, and a frozen status line masked it until the next unexplained slowdown. The run owns that descendant, since it sits in the run's own process group or runs from under the run's own temp tree, so the run answers for it. At a stopping point the run reports a runaway descendant it provably owns: what it is, how much of a core it holds, and why the run owns it. That report is the minimum owed for this class, the notice word the owner gave (2026-07-17 ~16:58, the same word that ordered row 417's cleanup notice), so an unexpected burn is visible the moment it happens rather than at the next unexplained slowdown. It lives at the Stop surface beside the chat judges and takes no push-gate letter, because a push gate runs long after the runaway would have burned its cores. Because it runs in process space, where a coarse scope does real harm — the broad name-based sweep that once closed the owner's real browser [INV-162] — a runaway is identified only by provable ownership and never by a program name: the mechanism `guardrails/check-runaway-child.py` reads the process table, and its core `find_runaways` reasons over process group, parent liveness, and processor share alone, reading no command or name field for its verdict, so a process whose command merely matches a known burner while sitting in a foreign process group and under no owned tree is never targeted. A runaway is a descendant that is owned (proved by process group or owned tree), orphaned (its owning parent no longer alive — reparented to init, or a parent absent from the live table — so a live-and-working child whose parent is alive is never one), and burning (its processor share at or above the host-settable threshold), with the mechanism itself and the group lead excluded from reporting themselves. It is notice-first: it reports through the shared cleanup-notice module `guardrails/cleanup_notice.py` [INV-204] and ends no process, so the mechanism can never become the broad-sweep footgun it guards against; a reap gated on the same strict ownership proof is a later, optional step. Its live wiring is a documented owner-run install step rather than an auto-wire into a running session's Stop hook, since wiring a process scanner into a live session mid-movement could report against that session's own live background workers. This is the cleanup-notice discipline [INV-204] and the owned-identity discipline [INV-162] applied to an orphaned worker descendant. [INV-213]

- **A worker's teardown reaps its own process group, and a stalled worker is caught by its idle output.** INV-213 reports an owned runaway and ends nothing; this lands the reap that report deferred and the detection habit that finds a stall before a frozen status line hides it. Teardown carries two duties beside completing the agent: the agent completes, and the process group the run itself spawned is reaped, so a heavy or blocked child — a pathological diff, a hung heredoc, a stuck browser — cannot outlive the agent. The reap is scoped to the run's own group and safe for that reason [INV-162]: `guardrails/reap_owned_group.py`'s `reap_owned_group` takes a numeric process group and refuses any group absent from the run's owned set, so a program name is not a legal target and the broad name-based sweep that once closed the owner's real browser has no door here [base rule 17]; it signals the group through `os.killpg`, the run having started its children into their own group so the reaper stands outside it, and it reports what it ended through the shared cleanup-notice shape [INV-204] the way every ending says what it ended. The idle-output detection habit stands in the worker contract [ACT-3]: a worker whose status reads "running" while its output file has stopped growing is read by that file's mtime — the liveness-via-mtime read [INV-76] — and `find_idle_output_workers` returns the stalled workers each with its owned process group, so the session confirms with `ps` and reaps the owned group. The memory instance is a worker that finished forty-eight minutes before anyone noticed while a difflib child burned a core under a status line still reading "running" (2026-07-17). Detection and reap stay two steps, and only an owned group is ever reaped: the module proves the reap is scoped to the run's own group or it ends nothing. It is a process-space habit at the worker's teardown and takes no push-gate letter, the way the runaway-child notice takes none [INV-213]. This is the reap and detection arms of the runaway-child class [INV-213], the owned-identity [INV-162] and cleanup-notice [INV-204] disciplines applied to a worker's own process group. [INV-230]

- **A permission rule that points at nothing is a dead rule, and config-health reads it.** A permission rule the harness enforces can name a filesystem path — a deploy script, an editable tree, a browser binary — and a rule whose path no longer exists still sits in the settings looking correct while it enforces nothing; a stale allow rule fails exactly like a missing one, so every action it was meant to permit falls through to a prompt and no one can see why. The worked instance: the owner reported (2026-07-17 ~15:29) that the harness sometimes refused a push or a deploy, and three deploy permissions were found still written against `~/tlvphoto` after the tree was renamed to `~/tlvphotos` on 2026-07-10, so for a week those rules pointed at a path that no longer existed, silently dead. So config-health (gate m) gains an arm, `guardrails/check-config-health-perms.py`, that resolves every filesystem path named inside a permission rule in the personal `~/.claude/settings.json` and the host's project settings and reds a rule whose path is absent — a rename anywhere on the machine then reds at the next gate rather than degrading into prompts. The arm reads absolute and `~/`-rooted paths, strips a trailing glob to its literal ancestor, keeps a path with a space whole rather than splitting it into a missing prefix, and reports the count of rules it resolved, so a rule shape it cannot resolve is named rather than silently skipped [INV-176]. The permissions are personal-layer, so the arm runs where those settings exist and stands down honestly by name where it cannot read them: an absent settings file is a legitimate stand-down, a present-but-unreadable one reds so it never falsely passes, the same shape config-health already uses to skip a CI checkout. It rides gate m's existing CI carve-out and gate m's known-red proof, adding no gate letter. This is a structural scan kin of config-health [INV-175], the CI-mirror gate [INV-210], and the judge-listed gate [INV-211]: those prove a hook file and its wiring exist, and this proves the path a permission rule names still exists. [INV-216]

- **The snapshot [target: the machine; the design is decided]** — the saved artifact of the last accepted run: HTML, JSON, files, numbers. The next run diffs against it as the baseline [E-7].
  - Lives in `.live-spec/snapshot/`: one folder per declared surface, plus one manifest line per surface recording what it is, the landing that set it (row, date), and a content hash — the attic manifest's sibling.
  - The baseline only advances at *landed*, and only for the surfaces the change declared; undeclared surfaces keep their old baseline. That asymmetry catches the unasked change: the guardrails' declared-scope check [E-6] goes red when a rendered surface differs from its baseline but the landing never declared it.
  - Adoption saves the first baseline from the artifacts as found [A-6]. The working tree keeps only the last baseline; git history is the archive. The snapshot folder is git-tracked, and of `.live-spec/` only the checkpoints stay ignored [E-8], so any older baseline can be checked out.
  - A too-heavy surface keeps only its manifest line and hash in git; the bytes live outside, and only the hash gets diffed.

  The machine's design is decided; it stays [target] until its first mechanical slice lands, riding the guardrails scaffold.

- **Design-sync [target: the machine; the wiring is live]** — an optional machine for hosts with visual components [E-18]. It syncs the components a landing declared — the same declared-scope notion the snapshot diffs by [E-7] — to the team's design project (claude.ai/design), where the human reviews rendered cards. It supplements the in-session render: the real render stays the authority for the landing gate; the design project is just the team-review channel.
  - Wired today (row 93's pack-side half): the switch lives off-by-default in the base skill's defaults table [E-13], under the name `design-sync`. A host that turns it on writes a recorded profile line [INV-14], and the channel lines stand in communicator and in the pipeline's commit-and-show step.
  - Still [target]: the machine itself — the first real sync on a visual host closes row 93.

  Every sync is gated by the human, because a sync publishes outside the machine [ACT-1]. The pack itself, a text product, never syncs — the work-kind axis says so mechanically [T-16]: the machine applies to product-kind work on a visual host, and every other kind stands it down by name [INV-22].

- **The skill evals** — test the pack's own skills at the level that matters for a skill: behaviour [E-19].
  - Each working skill owns at least one recorded eval: a scenario where a bare session errs and the skill's text fixes it — the skill's own red-first test, proven red at authoring with a dated run record.
  - Evals live in `evals/` in the pack repo, one file per skill: the scenario prompt, the recorded bare failure (date + run record), what a with-skill run must show, and the checks a re-run walks.

  - A working skill without its eval is a defect the milestone audit flags.

  - The preferred form is executable [E-10]: the list lives as a declared map inside a completeness-gate test, so a mismatch is a failing test in both directions — rendered-but-unregistered, and registered-but-empty.
  - The `.md` file stays the honest fallback for a host with no test harness.

  - The completeness check scans the real rendered artifact against the list, so a surface that renders but isn't registered goes red — the registry is self-closing.
